What % of your ram should the Swap size be?

Depends. If the RAM is limited but the disk is huge 200%, If the disk is limited and there is plenty of RAM 0%. For desktop and laptop systems I usually use 50%. There is no good one-size-fits-all, if in doubt don't have any.

Swap is only useful as memory if the machine doesn't have enough. However in Linux, swap is used for more than just memory. Hibernation uses swap to store the contents of memory, fast temporary files (tmpfs) and perhaps a few other things. Hibernation requires it to be on a partition or some other place accessible before Linux boots. TempFS is temporary space that automagically will place files in either just memory or to a swapfile. Standard applications will already place temporary files under the same place "/tmp". It's also is useful for manual operations, I create any cdrom images in /tmp so I don't have to remember to delete them. So the size of RAM is still a reasonable amount for many desktops.
My rule of thumb is swap is twice the size of your RAM. My VM server has 16gb of RAM, so the swap partition is 32GB.

You see, this is actually where the arguments start.

When I was growing up, this was the standard. It's actually on the Arch Wiki, IIRC. It's the rule of thumb I use for all of my machines... Double the size of your RAM.

The problem is, with today's RAM capacities, is this necessary? I understand having enough SWAP space to house everything in your RAM, so that you don't lose data when you hibernate... But are we REALLY going to hibernate a machine with 64GB worth of RAM to move into SWAP? What about 128GB... or 256GB?

Where does it stop? I've heard some pretty compelling arguments that having more that 16GB is just too much... And I'm inclined to believe them.

When I first started playing with Linux (Slackware, kernel version 0.99pl12), a common bit of advice was at LEAST 1.5 times the amount of memory you had.

I can see the wisdom of using twice the amount of memory. I'd go with that recommendation, especially where disk is dirt cheap these days.
Fair enough but when I've got 2 TB of disk space, 32GB is a minimal impact

Oh, I understand that... I've got an 8TB in mine, and 32GB doesn't register on my radar.

But let's say I'm doing something that "owns" 32GB worth of data in my RAM... what could that be? I'm gaming? I'm actively compiling something? I'm transcoding a video of something? I'm editing/exporting a video?

Would I be hibernating during these times? Or would I wait until these types of tasks are done, inherently freeing up that RAM, and then hibernating my machine? Would I even need to utilize 32GB of SWAP space?
True. I know I'm not the norm, but I'm usually running a constant 3-4 VMs off my main workstation so having that swap is handy.

If you want to suspend to disk (maybe you use tuxonice), then your swap should be at least the amount of ram you have available to be safe. As you suspend to disk, the entire memory is written to the swap disk/partition.

You could also use less, for instance if you have 8GB of ram, and typically never use more than 4GB, you could create a 4GB swap partition and still suspend to disk properly.

These days disk swapping isn't common unless you have limited ram available. On a system with 8GB ram, if you didn't require ot suspend to disk, you could easily manage with 1GB swap if you wanted.

Having used Linux for a while now, and keeping track of swap use the whole time, I've never once seen swap use go over 100mb. I'm not saying it's not possible, but I honestly don't see a reason for the average user to have two times ram for swap. I'd say no more than 50% on it's own partition should do the trick for almost everyone on the desktop side - servers and true power users (graphic design, game devs, etc) may use more, but they should know enough to know what they need to begin with.
